author: A Robot
objectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars across the night sky during retrograde motion, including the eastward drift, westward loop, and return to eastward motion.
Explain why apparent retrograde motion occurs in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Contrast the geocentric and heliocentric explanations of retrograde motion and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Predict when retrograde motion will occur for a given outer planet based on the relative orbital positions of Earth and that planet.
Compare the apparent retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.description: Observe Mars's apparent retrograde motion from Earth's viewpoint. Watch as Mars traces a westward loop against the background constellations over the course of several weeks, demonstrating the phenomenon that challenged ancient astronomy.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the observed path of Mars in the night sky during retrograde motion.
Identify the three phases of retrograde motion: eastward drift, westward loop, and resumption of eastward drift.
Recognize retrograde motion as a key observational puzzle that motivated changes to astronomical models.
instructions: Watch as Mars moves across the night sky over the course of weeks.
Notice how Mars's motion changes direction, tracing a distinctive loop.
Pay attention to the constellations and how Mars's position changes relative to the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Establish the Earth-based observer and introduce the night sky background with Mars visible. Sets the initial observational context from Earth's surface.
clips.narration: For thousands of years, astronomers observed something puzzling: the planets normally drift slowly eastward against the background stars, but periodically they slow down, reverse direction, and trace a loop westward across the constellations before resuming their eastward motion. This is called retrograde motion. Let's watch Mars perform this dance as seen from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves gradually eastward across the starfield, simulating the apparent motion over weeks. Illustrates the normal phase of Mars's motion relative to background stars.
clips.narration: Night after night, Mars drifts eastward across the constellations. This slow, steady eastward motion continues for many months. We call this the direct motion of Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars visibly slows and begins its westward loop motion. Demonstrates the transition from direct to retrograde motion and the characteristic loop shape.
clips.narration: But then something remarkable happens. Mars slows its eastward motion, stops, and begins to move westward—backward across the sky. For about two months, Mars traces a distinctive retrograde loop, moving westward against the starry background.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars curves back and resumes eastward motion. Shows the completion of the retrograde cycle and reopens the central question motivating the lab.
clips.narration: After about two months of westward motion, Mars stops its backward movement, turns around again, and resumes its slow eastward drift across the constellations. This cycle repeats roughly every 26 months for Mars. The question that puzzled ancient astronomers is simple but profound: why?

modules.moduleName: The Heliocentric Solution: A View from Above
modules.description: Step outside the solar system and observe both Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun. See how retrograde motion emerges naturally from the relative motions of these two planets—a consequence of Earth's faster orbit overtaking Mars's slower orbit.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain retrograde motion as a geometric consequence of relative orbital motion.
Describe how Earth's faster inner orbit causes it to periodically overtake the slower-moving outer planet Mars.
Demonstrate that the retrograde loop is an illusion of perspective, not a real reversal of planetary motion.
Understand why the heliocentric model explains retrograde motion more parsimoniously than the geocentric model.
instructions: View the solar system from an external perspective, looking down at the orbital planes.
Watch how Earth and Mars move along their orbits at different speeds.
Notice how Earth's faster motion causes it to pass Mars, creating the apparent loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the heliocentric model with the Sun at the center and two planets in their orbits. Establishes the external viewpoint and emphasizes the speed difference between the planets.
clips.narration: Now let's shift our perspective. Imagine stepping outside the solar system and looking down at Earth and Mars as they orbit the Sun. Both planets move in the same direction—counterclockwise—around the Sun. But they move at different speeds. Earth, being closer to the Sun, orbits faster than the distant Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Both planets orbit at their different rates, with Earth completing its orbit faster. The animation shows Earth gradually moving from behind Mars to ahead of Mars, simulating the overtaking process.
clips.narration: Watch what happens over time. Earth, moving faster on its inner orbit, gradually catches up to Mars. Eventually, Earth passes Mars—it overtakes the slower-moving outer planet. From Earth's perspective, this creates the illusion that Mars is moving backward against the background stars. But Mars is not actually reversing; it's Earth that is passing it!

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasize the geometric illusion through the car analogy. Highlights the simplicity and power of the heliocentric explanation.
clips.narration: This is exactly like watching another car appear to drift backward as your car passes it on the highway. The car is not moving backward; your car is moving forward faster. The backward motion is an illusion created by relative perspective. In the same way, Mars's retrograde loop is purely a geometric consequence of relative orbital motion. No complicated epicycles are needed—just two planets orbiting at different speeds.

modules.moduleName: Comparing Outer Planets: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
modules.description: Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn to understand how the apparent loop size depends on a planet's distance from the Sun. More distant planets produce smaller, gentler retrograde loops because the relative-motion effect is diminished.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why more distant outer planets exhibit smaller retrograde loops.
Describe the retrograde characteristics of Jupiter and Saturn compared to Mars.
Predict the size and duration of retrograde motion based on orbital distance.
Connect retrograde loop size to the relative velocities of Earth and each outer planet.
instructions: Observe the retrograde loops of three outer planets side by side.
Notice how loop size varies with distance from the Sun.
Consider how orbital mechanics determines the angle and duration of retrograde motion.

components.text: Retrograde Loop Sizes Decrease with Distance

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce all three outer planets in their comparison. Shows the arrangement and establishes the foundation for analyzing loop size differences.
clips.narration: All outer planets exhibit retrograde motion, but the size and character of their retrograde loops depend on their distance from the Sun. Let's compare Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Each has its own orbital period and orbital distance, which determines how the relative-motion effect plays out.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight Mars's retrograde path as noticeably larger than the others. Emphasizes Mars's special role in astronomical history.
clips.narration: Mars, being relatively close to Earth's orbit, experiences a pronounced retrograde loop. The angle is large—Mars appears to loop significantly westward before resuming eastward motion. This dramatic loop is why ancient astronomers focused on Mars as the key to understanding planetary motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Reveal Jupiter's and Saturn's retrograde paths, showing their progressively smaller sizes. Demonstrates how orbital mechanics determines observable retrograde characteristics.
clips.narration: Jupiter and Saturn, being much farther from Earth, show smaller retrograde loops. Jupiter's loop is more modest than Mars's, and Saturn's is gentler still. As a planet orbits farther from the Sun, the relative-velocity difference between Earth and that planet becomes smaller, so the apparent loop shrinks. A very distant planet would show almost no retrograde motion at all.

clips.changeMeaning: Conclude with a synthesis emphasizing the explanatory power and parsimony of heliocentrism. Ties all three planets back to the core conceptual point.
clips.narration: This elegant pattern is exactly what the heliocentric model predicts. The geocentric model, by contrast, required ever more complicated epicycles—little loops within loops—to match observations of each planet. With the Sun at the center and planets orbiting at different speeds, retrograde motion becomes simple: it's just relative motion. This simplicity is a key reason why the heliocentric model triumphed.
